title: Alexander and the Gordian Knot
text:
In the spring of 333 BC, Alexander reached Gordium, the old capital of Phrygia, on his march into Asia. In the citadel stood an ancient ox cart said to have belonged to Gordius, the peasant who became king, or to his son Midas. Its yoke was tied to the pole with a knot of cornel bark so tangled that no one could find where it began or ended. A prophecy said that whoever untied it would rule Asia.

Alexander could not walk away from such a test with his army watching. Arrian reports two versions of what happened. In the more famous one, Alexander, unable to find the ends, drew his sword and cut through the knot. Aristobulus, who served on the campaign, said instead that he pulled out the peg that held the yoke to the pole and slid the yoke free. Plutarch repeats both accounts.

Either way, Alexander declared the prophecy fulfilled, and Arrian adds that thunder and lightning that night were taken as a sign of the gods' approval. He offered sacrifices and moved on. Within a few years he had defeated Darius and ruled the Persian Empire from Egypt to the Indus.
lesson: When a problem is defined by rules that make it unsolvable, ask whether the rules are really binding. A fresh angle can turn an impossible puzzle into a simple task.
source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.3; Plutarch, Life of Alexander 18
caveat: The ancient sources disagree on whether Alexander cut the knot or removed the pole pin, and the prophecy itself is legend.
